Confidence Interval for the Square Root of the Signal-to-Noise Ratio

Source: R/ci_srsnr.R
ci_srsnr.Rd

Computes the exact confidence interval for the square root of the signal-to-noise ratio, the standard deviation of the group means relative to the error standard deviation. On this root scale the quantity is an effect size in standard deviation units, the multi-group analog of the standardized mean difference.

Usage

ci_srsnr(
  F_value = NULL,
  df_1 = NULL,
  df_2 = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  means = NULL,
  var_within = NULL,
  n_per_group = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

F_value

Observed F-value from the analysis of variance. Use this argument when re-analyzing existing data.

df_1

Numerator degrees of freedom

df_2

Denominator degrees of freedom

N

Sample size

means

Numeric vector of group means, one per group and at least two, given with var_within and n_per_group in place of F_value: the observed sample means of a one-way design, from which the function computes the observed F, or population means for a hypothetical interval (see Details).

var_within

The within-group variance that goes with means, a single positive number: the pooled within-group mean square (the mean square error of the one-way analysis of variance), or a population within-group variance for a hypothetical interval.

n_per_group

The group sizes that go with means: a single size for equal groups, or one size per group, each a whole number of at least 2.

conf_level

Confidence interval coverage (i.e., 1 - Type I error rate); default is .95

alpha_lower

Type I error for the lower confidence limit

alpha_upper

Type I error for the upper confidence limit. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound.

...

Allows one to potentially include parameter values for inner functions

Value

A 2-row data.frame with columns term and value. The term values are "ci_lower" and "ci_upper", giving the square roots of the corresponding signal-to-noise-ratio confidence limits.

Details

The confidence level is given in one of two ways: as the coverage, conf_level, or as the two tail areas, alpha_lower and alpha_upper.

The square root of the signal-to-noise ratio is the standard deviation of the group means, each weighted by its share of the total sample size \(n_j / N\), divided by the within-group standard deviation; it is \(\sqrt{\lambda / N}\) for the noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) of the F test, and it is Cohen's f with those weights (see cohen_f). This function uses the confidence interval transformation principle (Steiger, 2004) to transform the confidence limits for the noncentrality parameter to the confidence limits for the square root of the signal-to-noise ratio. The confidence interval for the noncentrality parameter itself is given by ci_nc_F.

The interval has two routes. The first takes the observed F, its degrees of freedom, and N. The second takes the group means \(\bar{y}_j\), the pooled within-group mean square \(MS_{within}\), and the group sizes \(n_j\) of a one-way design with k groups, and computes $$F = \frac{\sum_j n_j (\bar{y}_j - \bar{y})^2 / (k - 1)}{MS_{within}}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_j n_j \bar{y}_j,$$ with \(df_1 = k - 1\), \(df_2 = N - k\), and \(N = \sum_j n_j\). With the observed sample means and mean square, this is the observed F, and the interval is the one the first route gives for the same data. Values of df_1, df_2, or N given with means must agree with these. Group means that are all equal give \(F = 0\), which is refused, as it is on the first route: at \(F = 0\) the upper confidence limit is undefined.

Population means and a population within-group variance can be given in the same places. The result is then a hypothetical interval: the interval a study with these group sizes would report if its sample means and its pooled within-group mean square equaled the values given. It is not an interval from observed data, and it is not the expected interval of such a study: the limits of the interval vary from sample to sample, and the interval computed at the population values need not equal their average.

References

Bargmann, R. E. (1970). Interpretation and use of a generalized discriminant function. In R. C. Bose, I. M. Chakravarti, P. C. Mahalanobis, C. R. Rao, & K. J. C. Smith (Eds.), Essays in probability and statistics (pp. 35–60). University of North Carolina Press.

Fleishman, A. I. (1980). Confidence intervals for correlation ratios. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 40(3), 659–670. doi:10.1177/001316448004000309

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F Test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the Analysis of Variance and Contrast Analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Venables, W. (1975). Calculation of confidence intervals for noncentrality parameters. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 37(3), 406–412. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1975.tb01554.x

Examples

## Bargmann (1970) gave an example of a one-way ANOVA with an observed
## F value of 11.2213 on 4 and 50 degrees of freedom, which Venables (1975),
## Fleishman (1980), and Steiger (2004) used in turn. Steiger describes it
## as five groups of 11 and reports F as 11.221, the value used here.
## The exact confidence interval for the square root of the signal-to-noise ratio of that example:

ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.541
#>  ci_upper 1.193
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55, conf_level = .90)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.594
#>  ci_upper 1.141
#> 
#> Confidence level: 90%

ci_srsnr(F_value = 11.221, df_1 = 4, df_2 = 50, N = 55, alpha_lower = .02, alpha_upper = .03)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.525
#>  ci_upper 1.180
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95% (unequal tail areas: 0.02 below the lower limit, 0.03 above the upper limit)

# The interval from the summaries of an observed one-way design: the
# group means, the pooled within-group mean square, and the group sizes
# of the three arms of drinks_trial. The F route gives the same interval
# for the same data.
fit <- stats::lm(log_drinks ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial)
ci_srsnr(means = tapply(drinks_trial$log_drinks, drinks_trial$treatment, mean),
         var_within = sum(stats::residuals(fit)^2) / stats::df.residual(fit),
         n_per_group = as.vector(table(drinks_trial$treatment)))
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.050
#>  ci_upper 0.510
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ci_srsnr(F_value = stats::anova(fit)[1, "F value"], df_1 = 2, df_2 = 85, N = 88)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.050
#>  ci_upper 0.510
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# A hypothetical interval: with population means of 94, 91, 92, and 83, a
# within-group variance of 67.375, and 20 per group, the interval a study
# would report if its summaries equaled these values. It is not the
# expected interval of that study.
ci_srsnr(means = c(94, 91, 92, 83), var_within = 67.375, n_per_group = 20)
#>  term     value
#>  ci_lower 0.238
#>  ci_upper 0.722
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
